_readme: This repo's own populated known-traps registry (issue #47 / backlog item #38-19), extracted from CLAUDE.md. Field contract: plugins/backend-suite/templates/known-traps.schema.json. Placed at the repo root rather than under .backend-suite/known-traps.json because this repo IS the plugin source, not a project that has adopted the suite — it has no .backend-suite/ directory of its own. A real consumer project's instance belongs at .backend-suite/known-traps.json, scaffolded by `plugins/backend-suite/bin/init.py`. Read this at the start of a session the way you would CLAUDE.md; it does not restate CLAUDE.md's prose so much as make it a queryable list of {trigger, trap, correctAction} rather than paragraphs a human has to remember to reread.

entries.title: main is the integration branch, not a place to commit
entries.trigger: About to commit, push, or merge directly against main — including for something that looks harmless like CI config or a docs-only change.
entries.trap: main gets a direct commit or merge that bypassed a feature branch and review, even though the change 'was small' or 'was just docs'.
entries.correctAction: Cut a feature branch from main for every change, no exceptions for size or category. Land changes through a branch and PR, never a direct commit to main.

entries.title: Every push, PR, and merge needs its own explicit go-ahead
entries.trigger: Already have approval to work on a branch, or to push it, and about to take the next step (push, then open a PR, then merge) without asking again.
entries.trap: One earlier approval gets treated as covering the whole sequence, so a push, PR, or merge happens that the user never actually signed off on for that specific step.
entries.correctAction: Ask for go-ahead again at the moment of each action: approval to work on a branch is not approval to push it; approval to push is not approval to open a PR; approval to open a PR is not approval to merge.

entries.title: The local run is the authority, not a fallback
entries.trigger: Finished a change and are checking whether it's safe to proceed — tempted to treat 'no CI check has failed yet' as a green light, or to run one verification script by hand and call that verified.
entries.trap: GitHub Actions is unavailable and staying that way, so a missing check is not a pass — nothing was verified at all. The subtler version: running `gates.py` alone, or reading an exit 0 while a step could not run, and reporting that as a clean tree. Every gate that ran passing is not the same claim as every gate having run.
entries.correctAction: Run the one entry point: `python3 plugins/backend-suite/bin/attest.py`. It runs all 18 gates (`run_tests.py` and `gate_consumer_compat.py` among them — do not run those separately) and reports the environment the verdict was reached under, because a local pass is a claim with conditions attached. Exit 0 verified, 1 a gate failed, 2 partial — and 2 is not a softer 0. Opt in to running it on every push with `install_prepush_hook.py` (`--uninstall` removes it; it never overwrites a hook it did not write). Use `gates.py -k` only while iterating, never as the verdict.

entries.title: A green local run is about your working tree, not the commit
entries.trigger: About to report a change verified, or to push, on the strength of a green `attest.py` run — with edits still uncommitted or files still untracked.
entries.trap: The local run is the authority now, but it is not equivalent to a clean-checkout CI run and differs in ways that matter: it reads the WORKING TREE (including untracked files a reviewer will never receive), the packages installed on this one machine, and one Python on one platform. `gate_consumer_compat.py` is the sharpest case — it diffs committed git blobs, so it is structurally blind to uncommitted work and can report clean on a tree whose pending edits are a consumer break. Reading a green run as 'CI would have passed' is a claim nothing established.
entries.correctAction: Commit first, then attest — so the tree being verified is the tree a reviewer receives. Read the ENVIRONMENT and LIMITS sections `attest.py` prints on every run, not only its last line; they name the conditions the verdict is conditional on. Treat exit 2 (partial) as a failure to verify, never as a pass, and never paper over a named skip.

entries.title: The main clone is often dirty with another session's work
entries.trigger: About to start work in the primary repo checkout — before staging, committing, stashing, or switching branches.
entries.trap: Another session's in-progress files get staged, committed, stashed, or clobbered by a switch, because the clone wasn't checked first and was assumed to be clean.
entries.correctAction: Run `git status` before doing anything. If it isn't clean on the branch you want, use a worktree (`git worktree add ../suite-<topic> main`) rather than stashing or switching. Never stage, commit, or stash a file you did not create.

entries.title: Regenerate, don't edit, anything generated
entries.trigger: About to hand-edit docs/CATALOG.md, or a template-coverage claim that reads like it came from templates/docs/roles.json.
entries.trap: A hand edit to a generated artefact drifts from its generator on the next run, and the doc ends up making a claim about the plugin's contents that is simply wrong — this has happened three separate times with hand-written coverage claims.
entries.correctAction: Never hand-edit docs/CATALOG.md — regenerate it via `bin/catalog.py` from component frontmatter. Never hand-write template coverage counts — they come from templates/docs/roles.json.

entries.title: No project literal may appear in the universal plugin
entries.trigger: Writing a new skill, agent, hook, or script under plugins/backend-suite/, and about to write a literal path, filename, or the consuming project's own name/framework detail directly into it (e.g. `docs/DESIGN.md`, `lib/`, `pubspec.yaml`, a hardcoded language regex, a project's accepted-exception constant).
entries.trap: The component works for the one project it was written against and silently misbehaves or refuses on every other consumer, because it baked in that project's shape instead of reading it from configuration.
entries.correctAction: Route project-specific facts through configuration instead: `{{doc:design}}` resolved via bin/resolve.py (not a literal doc path), `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/...` (not a project-local script path), `.backend-suite/profile.json` (not a hardcoded lib/asset path), "this project" or profile.project.name (not the consumer's real name), a module in backend_suite/adapters/ (not a language-specific regex inline), `.backend-suite/exceptions.json` (not a baked-in accepted-exception constant).

entries.title: house-style ships its own resolve_role.py — don't extend the wrong copy
entries.trigger: Adding doc-role resolution logic and about to edit whichever resolve.py-shaped file is closest at hand, inside the house-style plugin.
entries.trap: house-style is org-scope and cannot reach backend-suite's resolver across the plugin cache's per-plugin version hashes, so it carries its own parity-tested bin/resolve_role.py. Extending the wrong one either has no effect for that plugin or creates two resolvers that quietly diverge.
entries.correctAction: Extend plugins/backend-suite/bin/resolve.py for backend-suite consumers. For house-style specifically, extend its own bin/resolve_role.py and keep it parity-tested against resolve.py — never let the two drift.

entries.title: A 0-finding baseline proves nothing before or after a refactor
entries.trigger: About to claim a refactor was behaviour-preserving on the strength of an audit reporting 0 findings both before and after.
entries.trap: 0-before and 0-after look identical whether the check actually works or is silently broken (e.g. self-skipping because it can't find what it's meant to scan) — a clean diff is not evidence the audit ran at all.
entries.correctAction: Capture the oracle first with `bash plugins/backend-suite/bin/capture-baselines.sh`, then plant a broken file and confirm the audit actually catches it before trusting a 0-finding result as meaningful.

entries.title: Component tier is decided by blast radius, not how hard it was to build
entries.trigger: Declaring a new component's invocation tier in its frontmatter and picking `auto` because the component seemed simple or low-effort to write. (The field is spelled `invocation`, not `tier` — `tier` is the concept's name in prose, and a frontmatter key by that name does not exist and is silently ignored.)
entries.trap: A content-generating or convention-setting component gets marked `auto` and runs unattended, making changes (or setting conventions) across a project with nobody having agreed to them — the mistake wasn't in the code, it was in classifying blast radius by effort instead of consequence.
entries.correctAction: Every component declares `invocation` (`auto` / `explicit`) and `maturity` (`proven` / `unverified` / `experimental` / `pointer` / `disabled`) — the two vocabularies `catalog.py` actually reads and validates. Read-only and report-only stay `auto`; anything that generates content or sets a convention stays `explicit`, regardless of how simple it was to implement. `disabled` is not a confidence level: it means the component is switched off, its backing script refuses with exit 2, and every reporting surface must name it as disabled rather than letting its silence read as a pass.

entries.title: Local main can be behind origin, and ff-only will say it is up to date
entries.trigger: About to cut a branch from main, or verifying that a merge landed, after another session or a PR merged upstream.
entries.trap: `git checkout main && git merge --ff-only origin/main` prints 'Already up to date' while sitting on an older commit, because the remote-tracking ref itself is stale — no fetch has run. A branch cut here silently starts from the wrong base, and a post-merge check 'confirms' a merge that is not in the working tree. Observed twice in one session: once a generated file appeared reverted, once a just-merged PR looked absent.
entries.correctAction: Fetch first, then fast-forward: `git fetch origin main && git merge --ff-only origin/main`, and confirm with `git log --oneline -1` that HEAD is the commit you expect. 'Already up to date' against an unfetched ref is not evidence.
entries.source: Observed 2026-09-15; same shape as CLAUDE.md rule 4 (the main clone is often dirty with another session's work).

entries.title: Ignoring audit output by filename stops working the moment an audit is added
entries.trigger: Adding an ignore rule for generated audit output, or adding a new audit that writes a new findings file.
entries.trap: A .gitignore lists findings files individually (`token_pipeline/findings.json`, `a11y_findings.json`, …). A later audit writes a filename nobody added, so it is tracked and committed — and findings quote the source they matched, so this publishes code excerpts into a client repository. Measured: three enumerated, a fourth exposed with a verbatim `snippet` field.
entries.correctAction: Ignore a PATTERN, not a list of filenames — `<outputDir>/*findings*.json`. An allowlist-by-enumeration fails open exactly when nobody is thinking about .gitignore. `doctor.py`'s regenerable check reads the profile's declared output dir and reports any tracked findings file there.
entries.source: Observed 2026-09-15 in a consumer repo; check lives in bin/doctor.py check_regenerable_not_tracked.

entries.title: Acknowledging a consumer break without a migration note is a rubber stamp
entries.trigger: gate_consumer_compat.py is blocking a merge, and the quickest way past it looks like adding an entry to consumer-compat-acks.json that says the break is intended.
entries.trap: An acknowledgement with no `migration` path makes the gate pass while telling nobody what a consumer must actually DO — so an acknowledged break and an examined one become indistinguishable, which is the governing failure moved one level up into the escape hatch. PR #127 merged with eleven critical consumer-visible breaks (two audits newly exiting 2 while a client's CI invokes them by path, and a removed --require-resolution flag argparse turns into an exit-2 refusal) and every surface stayed quiet.
entries.correctAction: Write the whole entry, in the same commit that causes the break, so a reviewer reads the excuse next to the change: what the break is, which consumer invocation it hits, and the command/flag/config key/re-baseline a consumer needs. The loader refuses the entire file on an entry missing `migration` or `consumerInvocation` (exit 2, not a pass), and there is deliberately no --acknowledge flag — acknowledging must be a diff, never a side effect of running the tool. If the break is not actually intended, fix it instead; the escape exists because the pinning contract ships breaks in version bumps, not because breaks are cheap.
entries.source: PR #127, merged 2026-09-17; gate added the same day. Same shape as engine/ratchet.py's --accept-new refusal.

entries.title: An eval run without --scaffold fails every file grader, and it reads as a skill defect
entries.trigger: Reading an eval result where a family of cases scored low and many graders failed identically with `grader threw: grader focus file "<path>": path "<path>" does not exist` — and about to conclude the skill did not write the file.
entries.trap: `--scaffold` is off by default, so unless it was passed NO fixture is materialised for ANY case: every case runs against an empty working directory. Every file-target grader then errors rather than evaluating, and the run looks exactly like a skill that argued well and wrote nothing. The measured 2026-09-18 run is the worked example — all four `map-project-*` cases lost every file grader, including `not_contains` graders on fixtures (`app`, `pre-ratified`, `docs-site`) that really do ship a `.backend-suite/profile.json` and really do satisfy those patterns. A per-case fixture explanation cannot account for that; only 'no fixture was built at all' can. Chasing the per-case explanation costs a fixture rewrite that changes nothing about the score.
entries.correctAction: Discriminate before diagnosing: a `not_contains` grader CANNOT fail against a file that exists and lacks the pattern, so a failing `not_contains` on a file target proves the file was absent, not that the skill misbehaved. If the same file graders failed across cases using DIFFERENT fixtures, suspect the run, not the cases. Re-run with `claude plugin eval . --case '<family>-*' --scaffold` before changing any fixture, grader or skill. Confirm scaffolding by checking the fixture is on disk in the run's working directory — the result JSON does NOT record whether `--scaffold` was passed, so it cannot be recovered after the fact once the trace directory under /tmp is gone.
entries.enforcedBy: plugins/backend-suite/evals/README.md (documented only — nothing mechanically detects a no-scaffold run)
entries.source: Measured on eval run results/2026-09-18T03-06-49-269Z while investigating map-project-inferred-only scoring 0.17

entries.title: A case whose fixture cannot satisfy its graders fails BOTH arms, and reads as a bad skill
entries.trigger: Reading an eval result where one case scores low and its plugin and ablated arms are within noise of each other — and about to conclude the skill is weak at whatever that case tests.
entries.trap: A grader its fixture makes UNPASSABLE fails identically in both arms, so the delta is 0.00 and nothing in a results summary distinguishes it from a skill that simply did badly. Measured: `map-project-inferred-only` scored 0.17/0.175 in the complete clean run (`--scaffold` passed, fixtures materialised, zero skipped graders) because it used the `zero-state` fixture — 'source files and nothing else, no `.backend-suite/` at all' — while nine of its graders target `.backend-suite/profile.json` and its prompt asks for the mappings on disk. The skill is FORBIDDEN to create that file (`commands/map-project.md` Step 0; `bin/map_project.py` exits 2, 'refusing: no profile at ...'), so the case was unpassable by construction. This is a DIFFERENT failure from `eval-run-without-scaffold-reads-as-skill-defect` and survives fixing it: this trap's worked example is the run AFTER `--scaffold` was passed.
entries.correctAction: Read the delta, not just the score: a low score with a ~0.00 delta points at the case, a low score with a positive delta points at the skill. Then check the fixture against the graders directly — build it (`python3 plugins/backend-suite/evals/_fixtures/build_fixture.py <name> --dir /tmp/x --force`) and grep it for every file-target grader's pattern before blaming the model. Fix on the case side: re-point the case at an existing fixture that can satisfy it, and give the unsuitable fixture a case it IS right for. Never make the skill scaffold the missing file so a grader can pass, and never put a fixture inside a case directory — `eval_fixture_selftest.py` does not cover those, so they drift silently.
entries.enforcedBy: plugins/backend-suite/evals/README-bootstrap-and-map-project.md (documented only — nothing mechanically checks a fixture against its case's graders)
entries.source: Measured on the map-project-* batch ($7.04, zero errors, zero skipped graders): inferred-only 0.17 with / 0.175 without, against siblings at 0.85/0.65 and 0.83/0.63

entries.title: An eval suite run spends the same rate limit the session is using, and dies mid-suite
entries.trigger: About to run `claude plugin eval` over the whole suite, or wondering why a run reported dozens of `You've hit your session limit` errors and a suspiciously low cost.
entries.trap: `claude plugin eval` authenticates as you and draws on YOUR plan's rate limit — the same pool the interactive session is spending. A 20-case suite at the default 3 runs per case, with the with/without ablation on, is 120 model runs. It will exhaust the limit and take the session with it. Measured on 2026-09-18: a full run reported `partial=false` and $15.68, which reads like a cheap clean suite — but 45 of its runs had died with `exit 1: You've hit your session limit`, leaving 7 of 20 cases usable. The aggregate's `partial` flag is false because the HARNESS completed; it says nothing about whether the runs inside it did. Three suite runs across two days cost roughly $70 and produced one partially-usable result.
entries.correctAction: Run `python3 plugins/backend-suite/bin/eval_results_read.py <run-dir>` BEFORE quoting any score, rather than reading per-run `error` and `turns` out of `aggregate-result.json` by hand — that hand-reading discipline was written down right here and was still got wrong twice (issue #143) — a case whose runs all carry an error is VOID, not a result, and a turn count of 1 across every run means the arm died before acting. Budget the run: `--runs 1` removes the 3x multiplier, `--case '<glob>'` scopes it, and `--max-cost-usd` aborts at a ceiling rather than silently degrading. Do not start a suite run while the session is needed for anything else, and tell the user the quota cost before starting rather than after.
enforcedBy: plugins/backend-suite/bin/eval_results_read.py (a command, not a gate: results/ is gitignored, so there is no committed artifact to gate against. Run it on a results directory before quoting any score; it exits 1 on a VOID, ONE-ARMED or grader-skipped case and 2 when it cannot read the file at all)
entries.source: measured 2026-09-18: three suite runs, ~$70, 7 of 20 cases usable
entries.why: A run that dies partway still writes an aggregate with scores in it, and those scores are indistinguishable from real ones in the summary table. An absence-based grader credits an aborted run for free, so the wreckage reads as a partial pass rather than as nothing — the governing principle's own failure mode, in the tool used to verify everything else.

entries.title: A negative control that matches its own skill's vocabulary scores the plugin arm down
entries.trigger: About to write, or to trust, an eval grader that asserts an ABSENCE — `match: not_contains`, a `tool_used` bounded at `max: 0`, or an `llm` criteria file phrased only as a prohibition — where the thing being forbidden is something the model would naturally TALK about while refusing it.
entries.trap: Keyword patterns detect the TOPIC of the forbidden act, not the ACT. A correct refusal explains itself in the skill's own vocabulary, so the grader fires on it — and only the plugin arm has read that vocabulary, so the penalty lands on the arm that behaved correctly. Measured on `bootstrap-design-docs-undeclared-kind-stops-to-ask`: the pattern `(assum|default|treat)\w*[^.\n]{0,40}\bapp\b` fired on 13 of 17 correct-refusal phrasings, including "I did not assume the `app` archetype", and matched the skill file's own instruction ``Do not assume `app```. The entire delta of -0.22 in favour of the NO-plugin arm came from that one grader. Audited across the suite on 2026-09-23 (issue #136): 6 of the 12 prose negative controls had the same flaw, firing on 2 to 8 of their correct refusals each, and 3 of them matched their own skill's markdown. The failure is invisible in `aggregate-result.json` — it just shows the plugin looking worse.
entries.correctAction: Write the ACT, not the topic: anchor the claim to a sentence start, then allow only a run of characters containing no negator or hedge (`not`, `n't`, `never`, `cannot`, `no`, `nothing`, `rather`, `instead`, `unless`, `whether`, `if`, `would`, `could`, `refuse*`, `declin*`) before the claim itself — `plugins/backend-suite/evals/review-docs-zero-state-refusal/graders/no-clean-verdict.md` carries the worked form and the measurement. Then do both checks before shipping it: (1) build a corpus of correct-refusal phrasings and confirm the pattern fires on zero of them, reporting the hit rate on both polarities as numbers; (2) grep the pattern against the `commands/<skill>.md` or `agents/<agent>.md` it exercises — a hit means the grader can fire on a model quoting its own instructions. A pattern anchored to a literal structured report field (`Overall Recommendation:\s*PASS`) is the exception: it may legitimately match the skill's report template, because emitting that template line verbatim IS the violation. Where a regex genuinely cannot separate the act from the topic, use an `llm` grader with an explicit `PASS only if` clause instead — `design-auditor-undeclared-kind/graders/criteria.md` is the model. Never weaken the assertion to make it green.
entries.source: issue #136; measured 2026-09-23 over all 20 eval cases / 40 absence-shaped graders
entries.why: This is the governing principle turned on the measuring instrument. An audit that reports nothing must not look like a clean codebase; equally, a grader that fires on a correct answer must not look like a skill regression. Left alone it produces the worst possible signal — evidence that reading the skill makes the model worse — and that evidence is indistinguishable from a real defect.

entries.title: The no-project-literals gate only sees literals shaped like a directory
entries.trigger: About to read a clean run of `audit_skill_paths.py` as evidence that a file in plugins/backend-suite/ carries no consumer coupling — or writing a new literal into engine/bin code that identifies one engagement but is not a path: a service URL, a product or brand name in generated output, a package, an export symbol, a repository slug.
entries.trap: `PROJECT_PATH` is an alternation of DIRECTORY AND FILENAME shapes (`lib/`, `pubspec.yaml`, `mock_api/`). Anything that identifies one consumer without looking like a path is invisible to it, and the gate passes — which is the governing failure inside the gate that exists to prevent it. Measured three times, each a different costume of the same cause: `ds_flutter` (a package) and seven class names sat clean in /promote-component; a package name compiled into a `re.compile` literal sat clean in two sibling audits; and a consumer's mock server (`https://<uuid>.mock.pstmn.io`) plus that client's product name in a generated OpenAPI title sat clean in `generate_openapi.py` and shipped into every consumer's API reference. The UUID host is the sharpest case: it contains no project NAME, so the name rule could never have reached it either.
entries.correctAction: Read the rule list in `audit_skill_paths.py`'s module docstring before trusting a pass, and treat a new NON-path literal as ungated until you have checked which rule covers it. Rules 4–6 now cover the project name in a code literal, a repository slug, a configured export prefix and its package spelling, and an external URL host — each with a STRUCTURAL control (a configured prefix, a host allow-list) rather than a denylist of framework types. Deliberately still ungated, and named in the file so a pass is never read as portability: domain entity names (`MeasurementEntry` is indistinguishable in shape from `ThemeData` — listing them would put a copy of a consumer's domain model in the universal plugin), framework tool commands, and the owner segment of a URL in code. Before widening, MEASURE: run the candidate over the whole plugin and report a true/false-positive judgement per hit. A gate that flags many legitimate cases is switched off within a week, and a switched-off gate still reads as a pass — if the rate fails, write the trap down here instead of shipping it.
entries.source: Measured 2026-09-24 while scrubbing client-identifying material for hand-off to teams on other engagements. Rule 4-over-code and rule 6 each flagged 1 true positive over the whole plugin, with 0 false positives; the four URL literals in `*_test.py` are excluded by the file set, not by an exemption.
entries.why: A project literal is the one fact in a universal plugin that is true of exactly one engagement, and its failure signature is always the same: nothing errors, the component quietly points at somebody else's repository, server or product, and the run reads as clean. When that literal also names a client, the gate is a confidentiality control as well as a portability one — and a confidentiality control with a shape-based blind spot is worse than none, because it is trusted.

entries.title: An eval arm denied access to the plugin's own bin/ scores like a skill that skipped its script
entries.trigger: Reading an eval result where a case that depends on a `${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/bin/*.py` call (`scaffold_doc.py`, `resolve.py`, `map_project.py`) lost its `tool_used` / file graders, while `eval_results_read.py` still labels the case QUOTABLE with a live turn count.
entries.trap: Under the eval sandbox the agent runs in a non-interactive permission mode: Bash, Read and Glob calls that touch paths OUTSIDE the scaffolded workspace — including the plugin root itself — are denied ('Permission to use Bash has been denied because Claude Code is running in don't ask mode'), while the same tools inside the workspace succeed. The run has no `error`, plenty of turns and no skipped graders, so `eval_results_read.py` reports it QUOTABLE; the skill then reports honestly that it could not run its script, and every grader that expects that script's effect fails. Measured 2026-10-09 on `bootstrap-stub-is-debt-not-coverage` (with-arm 0.714 on 2026-09-23 -> 0.286 and 0.467 on two reruns, `scaffold_doc.py` invoked 0x, trace showed four plugin-root denials). Root cause, investigated 2026-10-09 (three reproductions): the eval harness runs the child in `dontAsk` mode, and the permission layer denies plugin-root paths even though the harness's own OS-sandbox `allowRead` lists the plugin root. Explicit `--allow-tools "Read(<plugin root>/**)"` grants, `Bash(python3 *)`, and evaluating the installed plugin all failed to lift it; a Write inside the workspace was also denied despite being granted. No managed settings were present. Not fixable from this repo or by an org setting: it is a harness gap to report upstream.
entries.correctAction: Before attributing a drop to a skill or to a recent PR, re-run the single case with `--keep-temp` and grep its `trace.jsonl` for `don't ask mode`. If plugin-root calls were denied, the result is environmental: report it as such, do not edit the case, grader or skill to fit it, and do not work around the permission policy. `--allow-tools Bash Write Edit` does not lift it.
entries.enforcedBy: documented only — eval_results_read.py does not inspect traces for permission denials
entries.source: Measured 2026-10-09 during the family-by-family re-run after PRs #158/#159 (claude 2.1.273); one kept trace inspected. Whether this denial was also present in the 2026-09-23 runs is unverified (their traces are gone).
entries.why: A denied tool call is a measurement that did not happen, and it is indistinguishable in the summary from a skill that chose not to act — the governing principle applied to the eval harness itself.
